co_unaweep_canyon.blurb: Unaweep Canyon cuts through the high desert southwest of Grand Junction, and it splits into two very different worlds. Nine Mile Hill holds the great majority of the climbing here: a huge spread of boulder problems, mostly easy to middling with a real tail of hard testpieces, set in a quiet, remote landscape of sandstone blocks. The main canyon is the opposite, with tall metamorphic walls of granite and gneiss, roughly 150 to over 900 feet, offering trad crack climbing mostly from 5.9 to 5.11 plus a modest amount of bolted sport. Expect solid stone in places and loose, blocky ground between the good sections. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons, shady blocks keep summer bouldering possible, and the sparse crowds suit climbers who like to explore.

ma_north_shore.blurb: The North Shore stretches along the coast north of Boston and is almost entirely a bouldering region, built on glacial boulders and short cliff bands of New England granite scattered through woodland. Lynn Woods, a municipal forest only a short drive from the city, packs in a thousand-plus problems across a dozen or so separate zones, from V0 up to the high end of the scale. Cape Ann, around Gloucester and Rockport, adds more boulders in wooded reserves along with a few small crags that carry a scattering of trad, top-rope and sport lines. Most problems fall between V0 and V6, with a thin tail of harder ones. The local ethic values clean natural lines over contrived eliminates, so climb accordingly.

wa_centraleast.blurb: This stretch of the eastern Cascades is centred on the Bavarian-style town of Leavenworth, where around fifty crags sit within a short drive. The stone is clean, solid granite, with slabs and cracks in Icicle Canyon and longer trad lines on the big walls along Tumwater Canyon. Trad leads the way, followed by a sizable bouldering scene and a fair amount of sport; most routes fall between 5.8 and 5.11, with a smaller number harder. Peshastin Pinnacles, just east, is a different beast: sandstone, mostly bolted friction slabs, handy when the canyon is wet. Farther afield, Roslyn, Chelan, Stuart-Enchantments and the Entiat range add alpine routes, scrambles and scattered rock, so the region suits everything from half-day cragging to bigger mountain days.

ca_san_diego_county.blurb: Climbing in San Diego County is spread across the city's suburbs and the sparsely settled backcountry to the east and toward the desert. There is no single flagship crag, just many good ones. The rock is mostly granitic, with the local granodiorite forming many key areas, while Mission Gorge and Otay offer a metamorphosed stone with its own feel. Bouldering is the biggest draw by count, followed by trad, sport and a healthy number of top-rope lines. Trad and sport routes cluster in the 5.9 to 5.12 range, and the boulders run from easy to hard. Climbing continues all year, but inland summers get hot, so people go early, chase shade, or wait for fall and mild winter days. Storms can make the backcountry harsh.

ny_adirondacks.blurb: The Adirondacks hold a broad mix of climbing in a forested mountain park, with the densest concentration around Keene Valley and Chapel Pond, and more scattered cliffs near Lake George, Lake Champlain, Indian Lake and the High Peaks. Trad dominates the rock, with multi-pitch lines from easy fifth class up through 5.11, and there is a good helping of sport, top-rope and bouldering. The stone is anorthosite, a rare rock that locals simply think of as granite, and it tends to exfoliate. Winter turns the region into an ice destination, with hundreds of waterfall and mixed lines, mostly in the WI3 to WI5 range, plus some easier scrambles and alpine outings. Ice is the cold-season draw; the rock climbs in the warmer months.

ca_san_bernardino_mountains.blurb: East of Los Angeles, the San Bernardino Mountains offer forested, mostly single-pitch climbing on granite, centred on Big Bear Lake, Running Springs and Lake Arrowhead. Bouldering, sport and trad are all well represented, and most routes land between 5.7 and 5.11, with a smaller number of harder lines; the boulders skew easy. The stone ranges from excellent to somewhat grainy, in the manner of Joshua Tree, and newer routes can be a little dirty. Holcomb Valley Pinnacles, high in the pines at roughly 7,400 to 7,600 feet, is the headline: heavily featured rock and plenty of friendly grades. Highway 38 crags, the north slope and Cajon Junction add smaller outings. Spring and fall are the most comfortable; summers run hot, so shaded cliffs are favoured.
